candidates.context: Identifying Trading Partners Under the Drug Supply Chain Security Act Guidance for Industry DRAFT GUIDANCE This guidance document is being distributed for comment purposes only.

candidates.statement: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA or the Agency) is issuing this guidance to assist 17 industry and State and local governments in understanding how to categorize the entities in the 18 drug supply chain in accordance with the Drug Supply Chain Security Act (DSCSA). 2 DSCSA 19 establishes product tracing requirements for certain trading partners in the drug supply chain, 20 including manufacturers, repackagers, wholesale distributors, and dispensers. DSCSA also 21 requires that trading partners of manufacturers, wholesale distributors, dispensers, and 22 repackagers must meet the applicable requirements for being “authorized trading partners.” 3
candidates.context: DSCSA also requires FDA to issue regulations that establish Federal standards for the licensing 24 of wholesale drug distributors (WDDs) and third-party logistics providers (3PLs). The Agency 25 is currently drafting these regulations. This guidance, when finalized, will explain FDA’s 26 current thinking on how licensing and certain other requirements apply to entities that may be 27 considered trading partners in the drug supply chain. 28

candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 39 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 40 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The use of 41 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but 42 not required. 43
candidates.context: 3 See sections 582(b)(3), (c)(3), (d)(3), and (e)(3) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 360eee-1).

candidates.statement: Section 503(e) of the FD&C Act (as amended by DSCSA) establishes licensure requirements 141 and adds reporting requirements for WDDs. Specifically, section 503(e)(1) prohibits a person 142 from engaging in wholesale distribution of prescription drugs in any State unless such person is 143 licensed by the State from which the drug is distributed, or by FDA if such State from which the 144 drug is distributed has not established a licensure requirement. Furthermore, under certain 145 circumstances, 9 such person must also be licensed by the State into which the drug is distributed. 146 Section 503(e)(2) of the FD&C Act requires WDDs to report certain information to FDA on an 147 annual basis, including State licensure information for each license, the name and address of 148 each licensed facility, and any significant disciplinary actions taken by a State or the Federal 149 government. 10
candidates.context: DSCSA also establishes new licensure and reporting requirements for wholesale distributors and 138 third-party logistics providers. 139 DSCSA adds section 584 to the FD&C Act; the section sets forth requirements for licensure and 152 reporting by 3PL facilities. Specifically, section 584(a) prohibits a 3PL in any State from 153 conducting activities in any State unless each facility of the 3PL is licensed by the State from 154 which the drug is distributed by the 3PL, or by FDA if the State from which the drug is 155 distributed by the 3PL has not established a licensure requirement. candidates.statement: FDA considers the situation described in paragraph (A) to be similar to a parent/subsidiary 249 business relationship (i.e., the parent has the power to control the business of the subsidiary). 250 FDA considers the situation described in paragraph (B) as describing a business relationship 251 where a third party controls the business of several entities, such as controlling both the parent 252 and the subsidiary. In other words, an affiliate is a business entity that legally controls another 253 business entity, directly or indirectly, or is controlled by another business entity; mere business 254 links or relationships are not sufficient to meet the definition of an affiliate . 17 Manufacturers and 255 their affiliates retain responsibility for carrying out the activities and requirements under section 256 582(b) of the FD&C Act. To be considered a manufacturer under DSCSA, an affiliate of a 257 manufacturer as defined in 581(10)(A) or (B) of the FD&C Act must have received the product 258 directly from such a manufacturer. 18

candidates.statement: DSCSA defines repackager in section 581(16) of the FD&C Act as “a person who owns or 263 operates an establishment that repacks and relabels a product or package for – (A) further sale; or 264 (B) distribution without a further transaction.” Under section 510 of the FD&C Act, and under 265 part 207, with some limited exceptions, any person who owns or operates any establishment that 266 manufactures, prepares, propagates, compounds, or processes drugs in the United States or that 267 are offered for import into the United States must be registered with the FDA. 19 This includes 268 repackagers of drugs. 20 Thus, such repackager establishments must be registered in accordance 269 with section 510 to be considered authorized trading partners. 270
candidates.context: B. Repackagers as Trading Partners Under DSCSA 261 An entity that falls within the definition of repackager in section 581(16) of the FD&C Act must 272 comply with the requirements under section 582(e) of the FD&C Act. However, FDA does not 273 consider a dispenser, specifically a pharmacy, that is solely engaged in packaging and labeling 274 drug product(s) for dispensing to an identified individual patient after the receipt of a valid 275 prescription for that patient (e.g., repackaging product into unit-dose packages for administration 276 to an identified individual patient), to be a repackager under DSCSA. Therefore, the 277 requirements in section 582(e) of the FD&C Act would not apply. 278

candidates.context: FDA has received comments and inquiries about how to determine whether a WDD is an 293 authorized trading partner. Comments have stated that one source of confusion is that DSCSA 294 provides a definition of wholesale distribution in section 503(e) of the FD&C Act and a 295 definition for wholesale distributor in section 581 of the FD&C Act that differ from the 296 respective definitions in the regulations promulgated pursuant to sections 503(c), (d), and (e) of 297 the FD&C Act, as enacted by the Prescription Drug Marketing Act of 1987 (PDMA). 21 Several 298 types of entities are not considered to be WDDs under DSCSA that were under these regulations. 299 Many of these entities are now considered to be 3PLs under DSCSA, and are discussed in the 300 next section. 301

candidates.statement: Jobbers : FDA considers a jobber to be a person or entity that owns or operates an establishment 315 that engages in wholesale distribution on a small scale, or sells product solely to retailers and 316 institutions. Jobbers engage in wholesale distribution because they own and direct the sale or 317 distribution of product to, and receive product from, a person other than a consumer or patient, 318 and are not otherwise excluded from the definition under section 503(e)(4) of the FD&C Act. 319 Jobbers are thus considered WDDs and are subject to the requirements for WDDs under DSCSA. 320
candidates.context: Generally, but with exclusions enumerated in section 503(e)(4), an entity engaged in the 310 distribution of a drug subject to section 503(b) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 353(b)) to someone 311 other than a consumer or patient and that the entity did not manufacture, would be engaged in 312 wholesale distribution and subject to all the WDD requirements under DSCSA. 313 D. 3PLs as Trading Partners Under DSCSA 322

candidates.statement: As it relates to the distribution of prescription drug products subject to DSCSA, FDA considers a 400 common carrier to be an entity that solely provides transportation services, 28 but does not take 401 ownership of the product nor direct the sale or disposition of the product. Common carriers do 402 not provide or coordinate warehousing for the products they transport. Although common 403 carriers accept and transfer direct possession of product, they do not store and handle product 404 from a facility, as defined above. Therefore, FDA would not consider the services provided by 405 common carriers to constitute other logistics services, and FDA would not consider common 406 carriers to be covered by the 3PL licensure requirements under DSCSA. The owner of the 407 product would remain responsible for compliance with any applicable storage and handling 408 requirements and for the product’s safety and integrity during transit, and should select common 409 carriers that can provide appropriate safeguards. 410
candidates.context: 28 Such transportation services may include the transport of product from one location to another, and cross-docking of product en route to its destination, but does not include the warehousing of a product that lacks an identified consignee or delivery destination.

candidates.statement: An entity that falls within the definition of dispenser in section 581(3) of the FD&C Act must 468 comply with the requirements under section 582(d) of the FD&C Act. The statutory requirement 469 for dispensers to exchange product tracing information became effective on July 1, 2015. 29
candidates.context: Under this definition, a dispenser is a pharmacy that does not act as a WDD, or any other person 461 authorized to dispense or administer human prescription drugs. Furthermore, this definition 462 redefines dispenser-affiliated warehouses and distribution centers as dispensers (these were 463 previously considered to be WDDs under PDMA). Such warehouses and distribution centers are 464 no longer considered WDDs, unless such facilities are also engaged in wholesale distribution 465 activities. 466 However, dispensers are not required to provide the product tracing information prior to, or at 471 the time of, a transaction if the product is dispensed to a patient or if it is a sale by a dispenser to 472 another dispenser to fulfill a “specific patient need.” 30 , 31 The term specific patient need refers to 473 the transfer of a product from one pharmacy to another to fill a prescription fo

candidates.statement: However, dispensers are not required to provide the product tracing information prior to, or at 471 the time of, a transaction if the product is dispensed to a patient or if it is a sale by a dispenser to 472 another dispenser to fulfill a “specific patient need.” 30 , 31 The term specific patient need refers to 473 the transfer of a product from one pharmacy to another to fill a prescription for an identified 474 patient. This term does not include the transfer of a product from one pharmacy to another for 475 the purpose of increasing or replenishing stock in anticipation of a potential need. 32 Although a 476 dispenser that sells a product to another dispenser to fulfill a specific patient need is not required 477 to provide product tracing information, other requirements of section 582(d) and the FD&C Act 478 may apply to the transferring and receiving pharmacies. Accordingly, such sales or transfers 479 should be documented by each pharmacy in a manner that would facilitate appropriate actions by 480 the pharmacy in the event of an investigation of suspect or illegitimate product, recall, or 481 notification of illegitimate product. Transfers of product to another dispenser without a specific 482 patient need may constitute wholesale distribution, subject to the requirements for wholesale 483 distributors in sections 503(e), 582, and 583 of the FD&C Act. 484
